front.title: Certificate Bundles and Encrypted Companions for Hardware-Backed Messaging Identities

abstract.t: This document describes a signed, compressed public certificate bundle used to restore hardware-backed messaging identities on another computer. A bundle carries S/MIME certificates, OpenPGP certificates, and bindings between public keys and device key references. A single-bank storage binding uses application data objects in a YubiKey PIV application, with a verified local recovery copy made before replacement. The public bundle excludes private keys and authentication credentials. A separate, authenticated encrypted companion carries software Ed448/X448 components for hardware that lacks those algorithms. An optional ultra-compact companion retains certificate structure and metadata while reconstructing eligible self-issued signatures once per host. The document specifies the deployed base payload and proposes a separately versioned extension payload for additional certificate types and explicit component-to-slot mappings. It is intended for the Independent Submission Stream as an Informational document.

note.name: Discussion and implementation status
note.t: This is a working draft, not an IETF consensus specification. Publication in a source repository does not constitute submission to the Internet-Draft repository or acceptance by the Independent Submissions Editor. Discussion and source: . The compressed single-bank base and full-companion formats have been tested with PQ Mail and a separate Sequoia-based reader. Ultra-compact implementation and validation status is reported in the Implementation and Interoperability Status section. The extension payload in this document is a proposal; deployed readers do not yet accept it. Only the current single-bank storage arrangement is specified. Historical encodings and storage arrangements are out of scope.

section.name: Introduction and Scope
section.t: A hardware token can hold private keys without holding enough public identity information for a new messaging client to use them. In particular, one OpenPGP composite key may involve two hardware slots, and an application may offer both pure post-quantum and composite S/MIME certificates over shared components. A public certificate bundle preserves certificates, their signatures, and their hardware bindings without exporting private keys.

For the public bundle, backup means writing public identity information to the device and restore means reading that information and creating local references to existing device keys. Neither operation generates, imports, moves, or deletes a private key. The separately specified encrypted companion can hold newly generated software components, but conversion between its full and ultra-compact forms MUST preserve existing component keys. An ultra-compact first restore reconstructs eligible self-issued certificate signatures; it does not create a CA-issued certificate or grant contact trust. These distinctions MUST be shown before requesting a private operation.

The abstract identity model consists of certificate keys, component roles, algorithms and explicit key references. A particular numeric slot layout is a provisioning convention for one device profile, not part of the meaning of certification, signing or decryption. A different documented card can implement the same roles with fewer or more key references, subject to its capabilities. The concrete storage and supported fixed-layout encodings below remain binding-specific; their presence does not claim that current clients already support arbitrary cards or mappings.

The device binding described here is application-specific. Its object identifiers are not allocations from the PIV standard. Other smart cards require a separately documented storage binding, sufficient storage, suitable key operations, and a means of retrieving or verifying public keys. Having a PKCS#11 interface alone does not satisfy those requirements. The format does not require a particular private-operation API.

section.name: Conventions and Terminology
section.t: The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, NOT RECOMMENDED, MAY, and OPTIONAL in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.

A profile pairs a signing certificate with an encryption certificate and optional OpenPGP material. A component is one constituent public key of a composite key. A slot is a PIV key reference, not a data-object identifier. A bank is the one manifest and its numbered data chunks. A binding identifies which existing device key implements a certificate key or component. Certificate validity, bundle integrity, live key matching, and correspondent trust are distinct results.

section.name: Encoding Layers and Limits
section.artwork:
PIV data objects manifest + numbered chunks PQMZIP01: zlib-compressed signed envelope PQMAILS1: payload + signer index + signature PQMAILB2: deployed base profiles PQMAILB3: proposed base profiles + extensions
Separate companion data objects manifest + numbered chunks PQMCZ001: zlib-compressed companion envelope signed body + ML-DSA-87 signature PQMCP001: full certificate + encrypted software P12 PQMCP002: reconstruction template + encrypted P12
section.t: All integers are unsigned, big-endian octet sequences. U8, U32, and U64 occupy one, four, and eight octets respectively. To match current implementations, a device serial is in 1..2147483647 and a generation is in 1..9223372036854775807. Lengths and counts MUST be checked before allocation, addition, multiplication, or slicing. Implementations MUST reject overflow, truncation, inconsistent counts, and trailing bytes at every defined layer.
section.artwork: BLOB(x) = U32(length(x)) || x || = octet concatenation MAGIC = exactly eight ASCII octets, without a terminator
section.t: The compressed object stream and the decompressed signed envelope MUST each be at most 65536 octets. A BLOB MUST fit within its enclosing structure and this limit. Zero-length BLOBs are allowed only where stated. A base profile count is 2..16, including at least one pure and one composite profile. These bounds are protocol limits, not a promise that a device has enough free storage. Writers MUST account for object overhead and other applications sharing device storage.

section.name: Compressed Container
section.t: The stream is one zlib stream containing a DEFLATE representation of the complete signed envelope. It is not a ZIP archive, gzip member, raw DEFLATE stream, or OpenPGP Compressed Data packet. A preset dictionary MUST NOT be used. Compression level is not fixed, so compressed bytes need not be reproducible.

The expanded length MUST be 1..65536 and MUST equal the actual output length. Readers MUST stop expansion at the declared bound, require end of stream and the zlib checksum, and reject additional output, concatenated streams, trailing compressed input, and dictionary requests. No decompressed data is trusted before envelope verification. An implementation SHOULD also bound CPU time.

section.name: Signed Envelope
section.t: The signer index is zero-based and selects a base profile's signing certificate. The signature covers the exact payload octets, including its magic and all lengths. It does not cover the envelope magic, signer index, compression, generation, or manifest. Verifiers MUST select the indicated key, determine the permitted signature algorithm from its SubjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI), and verify the supplied signature over the original payload bytes. Re-serialization before verification is prohibited.

The certificate issuer's signature algorithm is not the bundle signing algorithm. Pure ML-DSA uses the matching pure algorithm with an empty application context, not HashML-DSA. Composite signatures use the algorithm identified by the SPKI, including its prescribed hashing, domain separation, component ordering, and signature encoding. Implementations MUST verify every component. The bundle adds no separate signature context. Passing a precomputed external mu to hardware is an implementation detail and MUST produce the same signature semantics.

Writers SHOULD use the composite signing profile. Readers MAY require that profile by local policy, but MUST NOT silently accept only its classical component. Since the signer index is outside the signature, its integrity is conditional on successful verification with the selected key; it is not independently authenticated metadata.

section.name: Deployed Base Payload
section.artwork:
base_payload = "PQMAILB2" || U32(profile_count) || profile[profile_count]
profile = U32(device_serial) || U8(pq_sign_slot) || U8(classical_sign_slot) || U8(pq_decrypt_slot) || U8(classical_decrypt_slot) || BLOB(signing_certificate_der) || BLOB(encryption_certificate_der) || BLOB(openpgp_public_certificate) || BLOB(openpgp_v4_compatibility_certificate)
section.t: The X.509 BLOBs are nonempty and each contains exactly one DER certificate . They are not PEM, CMS SignedData, certificate chains, or private-key containers. The OpenPGP BLOBs contain binary public certificate packets, not ASCII armor or secret-key packets. Either OpenPGP field MAY be empty; a nonempty compatibility field requires a nonempty public certificate field. All original certificate packets, including certification and binding signatures, MUST be preserved.

All profiles MUST name the same device serial and the same four distinct slots. Pure and composite profiles MUST share the same ML-DSA and ML-KEM public components. A given slot MUST NOT be bound to different public keys anywhere in the payload. Duplicate signing/encryption certificate pairs are invalid. The current base profile places ML-DSA signing in 9c; the current creation layout uses 83, 9d, and 82 for the remaining fields in that order. PIV references are encoded as single octets, for example hexadecimal 83 is the octet 0x83, not the ASCII string "83".

Legal ordinary PIV references for base fields are 9a, 9c, 9d, 9e, and 82 through 95, hexadecimal. This range is syntax validation only: the four current role assignments and supported algorithm profile still have to match. Attestation and PIN/PUK references MUST NOT be treated as application keys. Importers MUST NOT move keys to satisfy a mapping.

section.name: S/MIME Algorithm Profiles
section.t: Each base profile uses one row of the following table, with the corresponding pure or composite form for both signing and encryption. The OID suffixes in the last two columns are relative to 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6. Level labels describe the ML-DSA category, not a certification of the complete system. In particular, ML-KEM-768 is category 3 in both the Level 2 and Level 3 profiles.

Pure ML-DSA SPKI OIDs are 2.16.840.1.101.3.4.3.17, .18, and .19 respectively; ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024 SPKI OIDs are 2.16.840.1.101.3.4.4.2 and .3. Their AlgorithmIdentifier parameters are absent. Composite identifiers and encodings follow the corresponding algorithm specifications . These identifier assignments are used, not allocated, by this document. Implementations MUST NOT equate similarly named experimental algorithms having different identifiers or encodings.

The first composite component maps to the PQ slot, and the second to the classical slot. Pure profiles map only their single component; the companion composite profile supplies the classical public keys. Readers MUST parse the algorithm's actual component encoding rather than treating the composite SPKI as a single device key.

Signing and encryption certificates MUST share at least one rfc822Name SAN mailbox. For activation as a messaging identity, validity periods and applicable KeyUsage and ExtendedKeyUsage restrictions MUST be checked; emailProtection or anyExtendedKeyUsage is required when an EKU restriction is present. Signing uses digitalSignature; the base ML-KEM/composite KEM profiles use keyEncipherment. Parsing a backup for inspection does not itself authorize use of expired or revoked credentials. CA path building and revocation policy remain the application's responsibility.

section.name: OpenPGP Content and Base Slot Bindings
section.t: OpenPGP certificates follow and supported algorithm profiles such as . Readers MUST validate self-certifications, subkey bindings, required signing-subkey back-signatures, key flags, and revocation/expiration policy before activating a key. A packet's presence alone does not authorize its use. Secret-Key and Secret-Subkey packets MUST be rejected. Unrecognized algorithms MUST NOT be guessed from lengths or replaced with classical operations.

For the currently tested Level 3 separated-certification profile, the base format uses the following fixed additional mappings. They are not additional fields in PQMAILB2. A reader MUST recognize this complete profile and match every public component before activating it, or report the profile as unsupported. The same logical public key may occur in more than one certificate view without implying another device key.

tr.td: v6 classical signing subkey / v4 primary

section.t: The v4 view uses the appropriate v4 packet encodings for its classical keys. A v6 certificate and a v4 certificate have different primary keys and fingerprints; correspondence MUST be verified by their certified identities and constituent public keys, not by assuming their fingerprints match. Unsupported OpenPGP profiles can be retained as opaque public backup data but MUST NOT become usable hardware identities.

A classical-only v4 view MAY be obtained by retaining the original primary key, User IDs and their certifications, and the classical encryption subkey with its existing binding signatures and relevant revocations, while omitting the hybrid encryption subkey and signatures pertaining to it. No signature is created and no PIN is needed. The primary-key fingerprint stays unchanged. Filtering MUST NOT remove a revocation or restriction applicable to a retained key, invent a binding, or silently change the selected cryptographic policy. The resulting view MUST be verified again.

section.name: Proposed Extension Payload
section.t: This section defines a proposed, separately versioned payload. It is not implemented by the deployed PQMAILB2 readers. A writer MUST NOT use it for an installation that has not explicitly enabled extension support. The single-bank storage, compression, and signed-envelope formats are unchanged. Unknown payload magic MUST cause a clear unsupported-format error; a reader MUST NOT strip extensions to try base verification.
section.artwork:
extended_payload = "PQMAILB3" || U32(profile_count) || profile[profile_count] || U32(extension_count) || extension[extension_count]
extension = BLOB(type_identifier) || U8(flags) || BLOB(value)
section.t: The profile encoding is exactly that in . Extension count is 0..32. Type identifiers are 1..192 ASCII octets containing an absolute HTTPS URI under the defining party's control. They are compared byte-for-byte, are unique within a payload, and MUST NOT be fetched or used as executable locations. Bit 0 of flags means critical; all other bits MUST be zero. Unknown critical extensions cause rejection of the entire payload. Unknown noncritical extensions MUST NOT affect usable identity, key selection, trust, or device commands. A reader MAY retain them as opaque signed bytes. A writer rewriting an imported bundle MUST preserve them or explicitly refuse the rewrite; silent loss is prohibited.

All extensions are covered by the envelope signature. Extensions MUST NOT override a base certificate, change its mapping, grant trust, designate an executable, supply credentials, or request provisioning. Conflicts cause rejection. The extension mechanism is additive: existing base S/MIME profiles remain required and continue to identify the envelope signer.

section.name: Additional Certificate Set
section.t: The type identifier is https://github.com/ve7jtb/pq-mail/spec/certificate-set/v1. The value is:
section.artwork:
U32(certificate_count) || certificate_record[certificate_count]
certificate_record = U32(certificate_id) || BLOB(format_identifier) || U32(purposes) || BLOB(certificate)
section.t: Count is 1..32. IDs are nonzero and unique within this set. Purposes is a bit mask: bit 0 signing, bit 1 decryption, bit 2 certification, bit 3 issuer-chain support. At least one bit MUST be set, other bits MUST be zero, and issuer-chain support MUST NOT be combined with other purposes. Purposes request local use and MUST NOT expand permissions in the certificate itself. Certificates are nonempty and public-only.

Format identifiers are 1..192 ASCII octets. This version defines the exact identifiers "x509-der" for one DER X.509 certificate and "openpgp-public" for one binary OpenPGP public certificate. Other formats use an absolute HTTPS URI and MUST define public-only syntax, key identification, signature validation, permitted uses, and component extraction. Unknown formats in a critical certificate set cause rejection. In a noncritical set they MAY be retained only as opaque data and MUST NOT be activated.

This extension can carry additional S/MIME signing/encryption certificates or issuer certificates without replacing the base pair. Issuer-chain certificates have no private-slot mapping and do not become trust anchors. The application still needs its ordinary S/MIME chain, identity, validity, key-usage, and revocation checks. A noncritical certificate set is suitable only for information that may safely be ignored.

section.name: Explicit Public-Key Mappings
section.t: The type identifier is https://github.com/ve7jtb/pq-mail/spec/key-mappings/v1. This extension MUST be critical, and its value is:
section.artwork:
U32(binding_count) || binding[binding_count]
binding = U32(certificate_id) || BLOB(key_selector) || U32(component_index) || U32(roles) || BLOB(locator_type) || BLOB(locator) || BLOB(component_spki_der)
section.t: Count is 1..64. Each certificate ID MUST refer to the certificate-set extension. For X.509, key_selector is empty and selects the subject public key. For OpenPGP it is the full binary fingerprint of the selected primary key or subkey, of the length defined for that key version; short key IDs are forbidden. A component index is zero-based in the order defined by the certificate algorithm; a noncomposite key has only index 0. It MUST NOT be inferred from field lengths. For example, OpenPGP wire order and an X.509 composite algorithm's order need not agree.

Roles uses bits 0 signing, 1 decryption, and 2 certification, with at least one bit set and no other bits. Roles MUST be a subset of the referenced certificate's requested purposes and its authenticated key flags/usages. A tuple (certificate_id, key_selector, component_index) MUST appear once only; several permitted roles are combined in that tuple. Every component of every key being activated MUST have a binding. No omitted component may be silently downgraded or synthesized.

The SPKI is the canonical DER encoding of the individual component, with the algorithm and parameters appropriate to that component. Readers MUST derive it from the referenced certificate key and compare it with both the supplied SPKI and the live device key. All bindings naming the same locator MUST agree on the public key. A binding that overlaps a base or fixed-profile mapping MUST agree with it exactly.

This version defines locator_type "piv-key-reference". Its locator is exactly one octet identifying an ordinary key slot on the same device serial as the base profiles. Other locator types use an absolute HTTPS URI and need a separate specification of device identification, key addressing, and safe public-key matching. An unsupported locator makes the critical extension unsupported. A locator MUST NOT contain a PIN, management key, executable path, PKCS#11 module path, arbitrary command, or remote callback URL.

A binding for another smart-card family MUST specify its locator syntax and version, stable device identification, supported key-reference range and capacity, certificate-component extraction, live public-key comparison, required private operations and authorization semantics, and a storage-object binding with collision and recovery rules. It MUST NOT assume that another card implements the YubiKey retired-slot range, current numerical layout, or custom data objects. A device with insufficient references or an unsupported algorithm MUST be reported as unsupported; roles MUST NOT be silently merged or replaced by software. Existing fixed-profile readers MUST reject an unsupported mapping revision instead of applying their own slot defaults.

The proposed B3 extension describes additional explicit mappings but still includes the base profile's required fields and constraints. A card family that cannot represent those fields, device identifier or algorithms needs a separately versioned payload/profile specification; a new locator string alone does not remove those constraints. Likewise, the current encrypted-companion implementation below recognizes only its named fixed mapping. General role-based restore must be implemented and tested before claiming support for a new card binding.

These mappings permit additional S/MIME certificates, multiple OpenPGP keys, and other specified certificate formats without assuming particular PIV slots. They do not enable a device algorithm, change touch/PIN policy, or prove a private key is nonexportable. Import MUST show the proposed mappings for user review.

section.name: Single-Bank PIV Storage Binding
section.t: The YubiKey PIV application documents application-defined GET DATA and PUT DATA objects . This binding uses object 0x5f5000 for the manifest and objects 0x5f5001 through 0x5f5020 for up to 32 chunks. These are application conventions, not globally reserved tags. Writers MUST detect namespace collisions and MUST NOT overwrite unrelated or unrecognized data. Standard PIV certificate objects are not used for the bundle.

Object values below exclude APDU framing, status words, and PIV data-object TLV wrappers. A transport adapter MUST remove only those wrappers, assemble ISO 7816 response chaining correctly, and supply exact object bytes. USB and NFC must yield identical bytes. Only an explicit object-not-found result is absence; permission failures, tag loss, timeouts, malformed responses, and transport errors MUST remain errors.
section.artwork:
manifest (52 octets): "PQMIDX01" || U64(generation) || U32(stored_length) || SHA256(compressed)
chunk i at object 0x5f5001 + i: "PQMCHK01" || U64(generation) || U32(i) || chunk_data
section.t: Stored length is 1..65536. The number of chunks is ceiling(stored_length / 2048), at most 32. Index i starts at zero. Every chunk except the last carries exactly 2048 data octets; the last carries precisely the remaining 1..2048 octets. All chunk generations MUST equal the manifest generation. The digest covers the concatenated compressed data, not the chunk headers. Its purpose is complete-object consistency checking, not authentication or rollback protection.

A successful write retains only this bank. No second on-card recovery copy is required or written. Unused tail chunk objects SHOULD be removed after local backup, subject to namespace ownership checks. Hardware keys, ordinary PIV certificate objects, PIN/PUK values, touch policies, and other applications MUST remain unchanged.

section.name: Read and Restore

ol.li: Read the manifest; reject invalid sizes or generations. Obtain each required chunk and require exact header and data lengths.
Concatenate data and verify the manifest digest. Re-read the manifest and require it to be byte-identical, or report concurrent modification.
Perform bounded decompression and parse the complete envelope and payload. Reject unsupported critical features and inconsistent mappings.
Verify the envelope signature and the certificate-specific bindings. Check all required live public keys and the device serial before offering hardware identity activation.

Show mailbox identities, full fingerprints, algorithms, device identifier, and slot mappings for review. Import public-only identities after confirmation; do not import trust, credentials, or executable settings.

section.t: Reading from a file can verify signatures without a card, but the result MUST be labeled not yet matched to hardware. A missing required key or a mismatch blocks hardware activation. Serial numbers are routing hints, not cryptographic device authentication. Public-key matching does not prove hardware provenance or private-key possession; those require separate attestation or an explicitly authorized private operation.

section.name: Replacement and Local Recovery

ol.li: Construct and validate the replacement payload, check device identity and every required public key, authorize bundle signing, and verify the resulting signature locally. Produce the compressed representation within the size bounds.
Snapshot every existing object in the owned bank. Refuse unrelated data or ambiguous ownership. If a complete prior bundle exists, verify and retain it as well.

Before any card mutation, save the original object bytes, verified prior envelope if available, replacement signed envelope, and replacement compressed bytes to a new local recovery directory. Include lengths and SHA-256 digests. Flush files, make directory entries durable where the platform permits, read the files back, and revalidate the replacement. If this cannot be completed, stop without card writes.

Obtain management authorization locally. Recheck the complete object snapshot, including absence of previously absent objects, and device identity before destructive work. Serialize access where supported; if the state has changed, stop and replan.

Delete or invalidate the manifest first, then remove the owned old chunks to release space. Do not treat a failed delete as success. Write each replacement chunk and verify its exact bytes by read-back.

Write the manifest last. Read the complete bank through the normal verification path, compare it with the intended replacement, and check live keys again. Record local completion only after success. Retain the local recovery copy.

section.t: There is deliberately no atomic availability guarantee during overwrite: removal, interruption, or storage failure can leave no valid on-card bundle. The UI MUST disclose this before backup. Automatic blind retries of a partially completed mutation are prohibited. An explicit recovery operation MUST inspect current device state and the saved recovery files, recheck keys, and obtain any required management authorization before rewriting. It MUST NOT regenerate keys or change touch/PIN policies.

The generation increments after a valid previous generation; the initial generation is 1. Writers MUST reject overflow. A resumed write without a valid manifest uses the generation saved in the recovery transaction. Generations are unauthenticated operational counters, not secure monotonic counters. An old valid signed bundle can be replayed; freshness needs separate trusted local state or an explicitly confirmed comparison.

Suggested recovery names are previous.pqkey, replacement.pqkey, replacement.pqmzip, object-TAG.bin, recovery.txt, and complete.txt. These names are local conventions, not wire fields. Directory permissions SHOULD limit disclosure of personal identity information. Files MUST NOT contain PINs, private keys, OAuth tokens, management secrets, or trusted-contact decisions. Recovery data MUST NOT be automatically published.

section.name: Encrypted Level 5 Software Companion
section.t: This optional companion supplies distinct software Ed448 certification and message-signing keys and an X448 decryption key while retaining ML-DSA-87 certification/signing and ML-KEM-1024 decryption on the device. It uses the RFC 9980 combinations, not a new message algorithm. It occupies a separate single bank and MUST NOT be placed in a public certificate field. A reader that does not implement this section MUST report the companion as unsupported; it MUST NOT substitute classical-only operations.

Full storage is the default. Ultra-compact storage is an explicit user choice for eligible self-issued OpenPGP certificates. It reduces on-device storage at the cost of a first-restore PIN/private-operation requirement. An application MAY convert an existing full companion after showing the measured size and restore requirements. Conversion MUST preserve hardware and software component keys, public-key packet bodies, fingerprints, slot bindings, certificate restrictions, and device PIN/touch policies. It MUST NOT regenerate an identity to make it fit.

section.name: Companion Envelope and Encryption
section.artwork: companion_stored = "PQMCZ001" || U32(expanded_length) || zlib_stream companion_envelope = BLOB(companion_body) || BLOB(signature) companion_body = companion_magic || U32(device_serial) || BLOB(certification_pq_spki) || BLOB(signing_pq_spki) || BLOB(decryption_pq_spki) || BLOB(wrapping_spki) || BLOB(certificate_representation) || BLOB(component_manifest) || ephemeral_point[97] || salt[32] || nonce[12] || BLOB(ciphertext_and_tag) companion_magic = "PQMCP001" / "PQMCP002" plaintext = BLOB(empty_password_pfx)
section.t: The compressed and expanded limits are each 65536 octets. The zlib boundary rules in apply, and nested compressed wrappers MUST be rejected. PQMCP001 carries one complete binary public OpenPGP certificate. PQMCP002 carries the reconstruction template in . Both are current optional representations, not successive certificate generations. Unknown magic MUST be rejected.

The four SPKIs are DER encodings for the existing keys in slots 86, 9c, 9d, and 82 respectively. They MUST identify ML-DSA-87, ML-DSA-87, ML-KEM-1024, and ECDH P-384. The public certificate's certification, signing, and encryption components MUST match those hardware keys and the software components declared by the manifest. Before any private operation, readers MUST compare the hardware SPKIs with the selected device and verify the envelope signature over the exact companion_body octets using the independently matched slot-86 key. The signature is a 4627-octet pure ML-DSA-87 signature with empty context; it is never omitted by ultra-compact encoding.

The wrapping point is an uncompressed P-384 point: 0x04 followed by the 48-octet x coordinate and 48-octet y coordinate. Readers MUST reject points not on the curve or at infinity. The writer generates a fresh ephemeral P-384 keypair, 32-octet salt and 12-octet nonce for each encrypted envelope. ECDH with the device's slot-82 public key gives the 48-octet, big-endian shared x coordinate, retaining leading zeros. The reader derives the same value with slot 82. An invalid or all-zero shared secret MUST be rejected.
section.artwork: AAD = companion_body through nonce, inclusive info = ASCII("PQMail companion P384 v1") || SHA256(AAD) key = HKDF-SHA256(salt, ECDH_secret, info, 32) ciphertext_and_tag = AES-256-GCM(key, nonce, AAD, plaintext)
section.t: HKDF uses Extract and Expand as specified by . AES-256-GCM uses a 16-octet authentication tag appended to its ciphertext . The ciphertext length prefix and envelope signature are outside AAD; the signature authenticates the complete body, including that length prefix and ciphertext. Every BLOB, including plaintext's PFX, MUST consume exactly its enclosing field. Authentication failure MUST release no private material to callers.

The PFX contains exactly three unencrypted private-key/certificate bag pairs, named cert-ed, sign-ed, and kem-x, with distinct Ed448, Ed448, and X448 keys respectively. The password is the empty string; there is no inner PFX MAC. The outer AES-GCM envelope provides confidentiality and integrity. Readers MUST reject duplicate/missing roles, extra private keys, unexpected encrypted bags, and private/public mismatches. The PFX and derived secrets MUST remain operation-scoped; no plaintext PFX, private-key cache or separately saved password is created.

Converting from PQMCP001 to PQMCP002 changes AAD. It therefore requires authorized unwrap and re-encryption of the same software keys with fresh ephemeral key, salt and nonce, followed by a new envelope signature. Unlike lossless zlib recompression, conversion does not preserve ciphertext or the envelope signature byte for byte. It preserves the key material and certificate semantics instead. An implementation MUST verify both the old and replacement envelopes and the exact key bindings before replacing storage.

section.name: Component Manifest
section.t: The component_manifest is UTF-8 JSON with exactly the fields version, serial, profile, and components, in that order, without insignificant whitespace. Version is the integer 1, serial is the envelope's device serial, and profile is the string LEVEL5_COMPANION. Each component has exactly role, algorithm, storage, slot, and sha256 in that order. sha256 is the lowercase 64-hex-digit SHA-256 digest of its DER SPKI. The array order and other string values are fixed by the following table. Unknown, duplicate or conflicting fields and noncanonical encodings MUST be rejected.

The serial is only a device-selection hint. Manifest validity requires the envelope signature, exact algorithm/role validation, certificate or template bindings, and live public-key comparison. Neither a serial nor a manifest declaration proves physical custody or hardware assurance.

section.name: Ultra-Compact Certificate Template
section.t: The initial template profile is deliberately narrow. It accepts one version-6 primary key with algorithm 31 (ML-DSA-87 + Ed448), one direct-key signature, one to five User IDs each followed by its positive self-certification, one distinct algorithm-31 signing subkey with a binding signature containing exactly one embedded primary-key-binding signature, and one algorithm-36 (ML-KEM-1024 + X448) encryption subkey with its binding signature. All signatures use version 6, algorithm 31, SHA-512 and a 32-octet salt. The certification and signing keys MUST have distinct ML-DSA-87 components and distinct Ed448 components. The packet sequence is:
section.artwork:
Public-Key(6), Signature(2: 0x1f), [User-ID(13), Signature(2: 0x13)]{1..5}, Public-Subkey(14: alg 31), Signature(2: 0x18), Public-Subkey(14: alg 36), Signature(2: 0x18)
The signing-subkey binding contains one hashed Embedded Signature subpacket (type 32) of signature type 0x19.
section.t: Conversion MUST begin with a fully verified certificate, including each certification, binding and embedded cross-certification. The template preserves exact public-key packet bodies, User ID bytes, algorithm identifiers, signature versions/types, hashed and unhashed metadata, creation and expiration values, key flags, preferences, critical bits, issuer fingerprints, and the signature-salt length. Per-signature random salt bytes are not identity metadata and are regenerated as described below. Packet headers MAY be normalized to definite-length new-format headers; this does not change key packet bodies or fingerprints.

For each eligible self-issued signature, replace its 4741-octet cryptographic value (114-octet Ed448 value followed by 4627-octet ML-DSA-87 value), its two-octet digest check prefix, and its 32-octet signature salt with zero octets of the same lengths. Apply the same rule recursively to the one embedded cross-certification. Nothing else is omitted. In particular, the full envelope authentication signature remains present. The resulting zero-filled template is compressed as part of the companion envelope. Its expanded length is not smaller; its compressed representation avoids storing those random-looking signature values.

Stored template packet headers MUST use the new-format tag octet followed by 0xff and a four-octet definite body length. Other valid definite-length packet headers in a verified cached certificate MAY be normalized to this framing for comparison. Partial-length, legacy-format, marker, padding, extra and reordered packets are not part of this template profile. Original subpacket framing inside signature metadata is preserved.

tr.td: 2 creation time; 3 signature expiration; 33 issuer fingerprint
9 key expiration; 11 symmetric preferences; 21 hash preferences; 22 compression preferences; 27 key flags; 30 features; 39 AEAD preferences
9, 27; exactly one type 32 embedded signature for the signing subkey only

section.t: Every signature MUST have zero unhashed-subpacket length, at most 8192 hashed-subpacket octets, one creation-time subpacket, and one exact version-6 issuer fingerprint. Duplicate types and unknown types, including unknown noncritical subpackets, MUST be rejected for this profile. Critical type 32 MUST be rejected. Other permitted subpacket critical bits are retained. The direct-key flags MUST be exactly 0x01, signing-subkey flags exactly 0x02, and encryption-subkey flags exactly 0x0c. An embedded signature is permitted only in its designated signing-subkey binding and is subject to the same version, algorithm, hash, salt, time and issuer rules.

Creation and expiration values occupy four octets. Signature creation MUST NOT predate the involved keys or exceed the current time by more than 300 seconds. A signature-expiration interval is relative to signature creation, and a key-expiration interval is relative to the subject key creation. Nonzero intervals MUST remain unexpired; zero means no expiration. Preferences 11, 21 and 22 have 1..32 octets drawn respectively from algorithm IDs {7,8,9}, {8,9,10,12,14}, and {0,1,2}. Feature subpacket 30 is one octet with no bits outside 0x0f. AEAD preference subpacket 39 has an even length from 2 through 32; each pair is a symmetric algorithm in {7,8,9} and an AEAD algorithm in {1,2,3}. These bounds deliberately restrict reconstruction eligibility; they do not redefine general OpenPGP validity.

User IDs MUST be valid UTF-8 of at most 1024 octets, each identifying one distinct email address, either directly or as a display name followed by an angle-bracketed address. There is no whitespace trimming. If the text ends with an angle-closing bracket and contains an angle-opening bracket, the address is the substring after the last opening bracket and before the final closing bracket; otherwise it is the complete User ID. The address has at most 254 ASCII characters and matches the application profile below. Duplicate detection compares the entire address after ASCII lowercasing, while preserving original User ID bytes. The same rules MUST be applied at conversion, reconstruction and cache verification. Unsupported identities remain in full storage. Implementations MUST NOT rewrite the original User ID bytes when creating a template.

This restricted address grammar is an eligibility check for reconstruction, not a complete mailbox syntax specification. ALPHA and DIGIT above mean ASCII letters and digits. General OpenPGP User IDs outside this grammar remain usable in full-certificate storage when otherwise valid.
section.artwork: sig_header = 0x06 || signature_type || 31 || 10 || U32(hashed_subpackets_length) || hashed_subpackets sig_digest = SHA512(signature_salt || signed_data || sig_header || 0x06 || 0xff || U32(length(sig_header)))
section.t: signed_data is derived from the exact key and User ID packet bodies using for the specific permitted signature type. The digest check prefix is the first two octets of sig_digest. Each reconstructed signature, including the embedded cross-certification, MUST use its own fresh 32-octet salt from a cryptographically secure random generator. Template normalization zeroes those salt bytes as well as signature values and digest prefixes, while retaining the salt-size octet. Readers MUST NOT sign using the zero placeholder salt or copy the old signature salt into a new signature. A reconstructed embedded signature is inserted before computing the containing binding's sig_header and digest. Both components of the resulting algorithm-31 signature MUST verify using the corresponding component keys before the complete certificate is accepted.

Fresh signature salts follow the security guidance in Section 13.2 of : re-signing a previously predictable digest forfeits the benefits of salted signatures, including resistance to certain repeated-signature fault attacks. This profile makes freshness mandatory. It preserves certificate identity and restrictions rather than reproducing the previous signature's randomness. Two valid cached certificates can therefore have different signature salts and values while normalizing to the same authenticated template.

A template is not a transferable OpenPGP certificate and MUST NOT be exported, attached to messages, or accepted as a valid certificate. The zero fields are defined placeholders only under PQMCP002; an all-zero signature in PQMCP001 is an invalid certificate. A reader MUST require the placeholders and their exact lengths, not interpret arbitrary signature bytes as a command to re-sign them.

This initial profile excludes third-party certifications, CA-issued certificates, revocations, unknown packet structures and unsupported signature metadata. Conversion MUST refuse such a certificate and retain its full representation; it MUST NOT strip those packets or signatures to obtain eligibility. CA-issued S/MIME certificates and chains in the public bundle are unaffected. A future extension that retains additional immutable signatures requires separate specified validation and interoperability testing.

The converter MUST preserve primary-key and subkey packet bodies exactly. Therefore their OpenPGP fingerprints remain unchanged. Reconstructed signature bytes and, because of embedded-signature dependencies, enclosing digest-check prefixes can differ. A pin on the hash of the entire certificate is not equivalent to a fingerprint pin and needs explicit handling. Reconstruction MUST NOT renew expiration, change an identity, broaden key usage, revive revoked material, or silently change the advertised algorithm.

section.name: First Restore and Public-Certificate Cache

ol.li: Read and verify the companion envelope and match every required live public key before requesting a PIN. Validate the entire template's allowed sequence, algorithms, metadata, issuer fingerprints, key roles, key flags, time/expiration constraints and cross-certification location. Reject malformed or unsupported records before any private operation.

If a local complete public certificate is available, verify all its signatures and policy constraints, derive its normalized zero-filled template, and require exact equality with the authenticated template. Match all primary/subkey fingerprints and component public keys. A valid matching cache avoids reconstruction. It does not bypass ordinary validity, revocation or trust decisions.

Otherwise explain that this host must reconstruct self-issued signatures once. Obtain local authorization, unwrap the companion using slot 82, and verify each software private/public pair. Recompute signature digests from the allowed packet structures and preserved metadata; never accept an arbitrary digest or message from the template as a signing request.

Regenerate the embedded 0x19 signature with the existing signing key before regenerating its enclosing 0x18 binding with the certification key. Preserve identity metadata, select a fresh salt independently for each new signature, and update derived digest-check prefixes. Regenerate the remaining eligible signatures with their proper certification key. Each resulting composite signature MUST verify in both components before use.

Parse and verify the complete reconstructed OpenPGP certificate, then normalize it again and require equality with the authenticated template. Cache only that public certificate, bound to the validated envelope/template and component keys. Clear operation PINs, unwrapped keys and temporary secrets. Do not grant contact trust.

section.t: Only the first restore on a host, or a missing/invalidated public cache, needs reconstruction. Subsequent signing/decryption still unwraps the companion privately for that operation; the cache does not contain software private keys. A matching already-issued public certificate can seed the cache without re-signing. A changed authenticated template invalidates the cache, even if the primary fingerprint stays the same. Implementations MUST validate the cache contents, not trust its filename, a bare fingerprint or an unauthenticated cached hash.

PIN and touch requirements are those of the existing device keys. A per-operation PIN cache can avoid asking the user again for each component, but MUST NOT weaken PIN Always, suppress a required touch, retry a rejected PIN, or change device policy. Certificate reconstruction is not a PIN-free public read and MUST be clearly distinguished from the full-format restore workflow.

section.name: Companion Storage and Recovery
section.artwork:
manifest at object 0x5f5200 (44 octets): "PQCIDX01" || U32(stored_length) || SHA256(companion_stored)
chunk i at object 0x5f5201 + i: "PQCCHK01" || U32(i) || chunk_data
section.t: There are at most 32 chunks, using objects 0x5f5201 through 0x5f5220. Each carries up to 2048 data octets; exact lengths and index rules follow without its generation field. The manifest digest covers the complete compressed companion. It is not authentication or rollback protection. This separate single bank MUST NOT overwrite the public bundle, ordinary PIV certificates, other applications, keys or policies.

The verified local-recovery and manifest-last rules in apply to companion creation, recompression and ultra-compact conversion. Recovery files MAY contain the encrypted companion, full public certificate and authenticated template, but MUST NOT contain plaintext private keys, PFX contents, PINs, wrapping secrets or management credentials. The writer MUST snapshot all 33 reserved objects, including absence, and detect unexpected tail objects. Recovery MUST compare current objects against the exact old/replacement journal and refuse unrelated data; it MUST NOT generate replacement identity keys.

Before ultra-compact replacement, the writer MUST verify that restored replacement keys and normalized certificate semantics equal the original, retain the original encrypted companion and complete public certificate locally, and make the recovery journal durable. Read-back MUST verify the new envelope and template and compare the committed bytes. Users can begin with full storage and explicitly convert later when shared device storage becomes constrained. The UI MUST report measured byte/object savings and actual free storage where available, rather than promising a fixed number of additional discoverable credentials.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: A public certificate bundle is public, not confidential. Anyone able to read its objects may learn mailbox addresses, device identifiers, certificate relationships, and key fingerprints. Compression does not conceal this information. Shared copies and local recovery files warrant the same privacy treatment as the certificates themselves.

A signature made by a key contained in the same bundle proves consistency with that key, not the owner's real-world identity. An attacker can create an entirely self-consistent replacement using the attacker's own keys. Live public-key checks and independently established correspondent trust are separate requirements. Restore MUST NOT automatically mark any mailbox/fingerprint pair trusted or turn included CA certificates into roots.

The public bundle MUST contain only public material and declarative mappings. Encrypted software private components are permitted only in the separately authenticated companion defined in . Implementations MUST reject private-key packets and prevent path traversal, executable configuration, automatic URL fetching, and command construction from certificate or extension data. Displayed identity strings require escaping and length limits. Import must stage all validation before persistent activation; failures MUST NOT leave partially trusted identities.

Signature-valid certificates can be expired, revoked, or unsuitable for the requested purpose. Removing a hybrid subkey can yield a still-valid classical certificate view. Therefore signature validity alone does not promise hybrid capabilities or authorize a downgrade. Applications MUST disclose classical fallback separately for signing and encryption and apply their local acceptance policy.

Storage ownership cannot be established by magic bytes alone. Before deleting, the writer must inspect the namespace and its application context; unexpected objects require explicit recovery review. The local recovery mechanism protects availability only to the extent the backup was durably saved and remains accessible. The unauthenticated manifest and generation permit denial of service and rollback. No claim of transactionality across power loss is made.

Readers MUST bound decompression, parsing, certificate counts, packet nesting, and signature work. Failed hardware reads MUST NOT be converted to missing objects or empty slots. Public-bundle and full-companion public inspection require no signing PIN or private operation. Ultra-compact certificate reconstruction requires explicitly authorized private operations as described in . An application MUST NOT retry a PIN after rejection or modify key policy to complete restore.

section.name: Algorithm Profiles and Private-Key Custody
section.t: An implementation can offer more than one algorithm and custody profile. An ML parameter set, a certificate algorithm, and the location of its private components are separate properties. The labels "Level 3" and "Level 5" below describe the intended post-quantum security category of the message-protection profile, using the specified composite construction and ML parameter set. They do not rate private-key storage, imply that every constituent algorithm has that security strength, claim that a complete implementation has been certified, or prove that private keys cannot be extracted. The message-level claim assumes secure key generation and uncompromised required key material; it is not the sum of the component strengths. Applications SHOULD display both the algorithms and the custody model.

tr.td: ML-DSA-65, ML-KEM-768, and the selected NIST-curve components on the device
Hardware custody for both components; the certificate protocol and implemented algorithm revision determine interoperability.
ML-DSA-87, ML-KEM-1024, and the selected NIST-curve components on the device
Higher ML parameter category with hardware custody; not interchangeable with the Edwards/Montgomery combinations in RFC 9980.
ML-DSA-87, Ed448, ML-KEM-1024, and X448 on the device
RFC 9980 combinations with hardware custody for both components; requires native device and transport support for every required operation.
ML-DSA-87 and ML-KEM-1024 on the device; newly generated Ed448/X448 private keys unwrapped into host memory per operation
RFC 9980 interoperability on hardware lacking Ed448/X448, at the cost of additional exposure of the classical private components on the host.

section.t: A NIST-curve composite used in S/MIME MUST NOT be labeled as an RFC 9980 OpenPGP composite. A separate experimental NIST/Brainpool OpenPGP encoding, if offered, needs its own explicit algorithm-revision label and peer support. OpenPGP version 6 alone does not imply support for every post-quantum or experimental composite algorithm. The native and software-companion Level 5 options use the same RFC 9980 message algorithms; their differing key custody is a local security property.

Hybrid signatures require successful verification of both components. A hybrid KEM uses its specified combiner and requires both component operations. A classical component provides protection if the post-quantum component suffers an unexpected cryptanalytic failure; conversely, the post-quantum component provides protection against breaks of the classical assumption, including quantum attacks. Implementations MUST NOT treat either component as optional, ignore a failed component, or silently fall back to a classical-only operation. Any robustness claim depends on the specified construction and its assumptions, not merely concatenating two keys.

The software-companion approach encrypts an empty-password PKCS#12 container in an authenticated envelope, unlocked with the existing P-384 ECDH device key. The envelope, rather than a PKCS#12 password, is the confidentiality and integrity boundary. Only ciphertext is intentionally persisted on the device and in local recovery files. The password is not a separate saved secret. This is classical protection of the companion at rest, not post-quantum protection of its contents. An attacker who breaks or obtains the wrapping key and obtains the ciphertext can recover the companion's classical private keys. That fact does not by itself reveal the hardware ML private keys or satisfy both components of a hybrid operation.

After unwrap, the Ed448/X448 private keys and derived secrets exist in client process memory. They may additionally be exposed through memory copies, CPU caches and side channels, debugging or process inspection, a compromised operating system, swap or page files, hibernation images, crash dumps, and diagnostic or virtual-machine snapshots. A design that intentionally writes no plaintext key files does not guarantee that no plaintext key material ever reaches persistent client storage. Managed runtimes and cryptographic providers may retain copies beyond the application's explicit buffer-clearing operations.

Companion implementations SHOULD minimize the lifetime and number of secret copies, clear owned secret buffers on success and failure, release provider key objects promptly, avoid persistent private-key caches, suppress secrets in logs and telemetry, and use platform memory-locking and dump-exclusion facilities where available. Such measures reduce exposure but do not establish the nonexportability of a hardware private key. Documentation MUST distinguish implemented controls from desired controls and MUST NOT claim guaranteed erasure when the runtime or operating system cannot provide it.

Touch and PIN authorization apply to particular device operations; they are not properties of an entire certificate. A no-touch P-384 unwrap can avoid an additional touch while the ML-DSA signing or ML-KEM decapsulation slot retains its existing touch policy. This does not put the software private keys under equivalent hardware custody or prevent their later use after host extraction. A conforming implementation MUST preserve device policy on restore and MUST NOT describe a per-operation PIN cache as changing a device's PIN Always policy.

There is no unconditional ordering between fully hardware-backed Level 3 and a Level 5 software companion. The latter uses higher ML parameters, while the former better isolates its classical private components from the host. The preferred option depends on the threat model, algorithm support, interoperability requirements, and device capabilities. Native Level 5 Ed448/X448 avoids the companion's private-key unwrap exposure when the required hardware and software support are available.

The public certificate bundle specified by this document MUST NOT contain the companion's private keys or PKCS#12 plaintext. The encrypted companion uses the separately authenticated format and storage namespace in . A manifest describing it must bind the device identifier, component public keys, algorithms, roles, storage locations, and slots. Restore MUST verify those bindings against the authenticated certificates and live device keys, and MUST reject unsupported components instead of substituting software keys or choosing a different profile. The serial number routes the request; public-key matching and signature validation establish the relevant cryptographic bindings. Ultra-compact reconstruction adds a signing-oracle risk if authenticated template fields are treated as arbitrary signing instructions. Independent structural and digest validation, strict role binding, and complete verification of reconstructed output are required. The envelope signature alone is not permission to sign arbitrary data.

section.name: Hardware Assurance and Key Generation
section.t: Hardware-backed storage is not a uniform assurance category. Devices differ in physical tamper protection, implementation quality, resistance to non-invasive and side-channel attacks, and lifecycle controls. FIPS 140-3 and Common Criteria evaluations provide structured assurance evidence, but their scopes differ. A product name, a PKCS#11 interface, an on-device-generation flag, or a vendor's use of the word "secure" does not establish those properties.

FIPS 140-3 validation applies to an identified cryptographic module, version, configuration, boundary, and approved services. Its security level is unrelated to the NIST post-quantum algorithm categories used for message protection. Common Criteria evaluation applies to a defined Target of Evaluation and its Security Target, possibly with conformance to a Protection Profile; an Evaluation Assurance Level alone does not enumerate which physical, side-channel, algorithm, or randomness claims were evaluated. An evaluation of a secure element is not automatically an evaluation of the complete token, its PIV application, or the host software.

Applications and deployments SHOULD examine the applicable validation certificate, security policy or Security Target, assurance scope, operational assumptions, hardware and firmware versions, and supported algorithms. Side-channel resistance MUST NOT be inferred solely from a headline FIPS level or Common Criteria assurance label. New PQ firmware, beta hardware, algorithms added after evaluation, or an unevaluated operating mode MUST NOT be described as covered without evidence that they are within the evaluated configuration. This document makes no FIPS or Common Criteria validation claim for the devices used in its interoperability tests.

Random-number generation is especially important when private keys are generated on the device: strong storage cannot repair a predictable private key. Relevant assurance includes the entropy source, conditioning, generator design, initialization and reseeding, and health tests. The NIST SP 800-90 series separates deterministic generators , entropy sources , and complete random-bit-generator constructions . A claim that a device has a hardware random-number generator is not by itself evidence of adequate entropy or correct use for every key-generation service.

A common failing or compromised randomness source may undermine both components of a hybrid keypair. Combining two algorithms does not compensate for predictable keys generated from inadequate entropy, and deriving several keys from one seed does not create independent entropy. Each component MUST be generated with a cryptographically appropriate generator and the entropy required by its algorithm. Newly generated software companion keys rely on the host generator and entropy source, not the token's key-generation assurance; the same applies to ephemeral wrapping keys and other host-generated secrets.

Restore verifies declared public-key bindings and does not independently establish the quality of historical randomness, nonexportability, physical protection, or side-channel resistance. Attestation may provide evidence of provenance or device state only within its own verified scope. User interfaces SHOULD distinguish message algorithms and categories, component storage locations, PIN/touch policies, and independently verified hardware-assurance information. Unverified assurance metadata in a signed bundle is a declaration by its signer, not a certification issued by an evaluation authority.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document requests no IANA actions. The PIV object tags and extension identifiers are application-specific conventions and do not reserve a PIV namespace, an IANA registry, an OID, a URI scheme, or a media type. Existing cryptographic identifiers retain their specifications. The local file suffixes .pqkey, .pqmzip and .pqcomp do not establish registered MIME types.

section.name: Implementation and Interoperability Status
section.t: As of 20 November 2026, a Level 3 bundle using the deployed base payload was written to a single bank on a PQC Ready YubiKey Beta0, restored into a fresh PQ Mail store, and independently read and verified with a Sequoia-based adapter. The tests compared public keys and PIN/touch policies before and after. This establishes interoperability for that tested profile, not universal hardware support or a production security audit.

The full Level 5 companion and its losslessly compressed storage have passed physical-device restore, signing and decryption tests in PQ Mail and the independent Sequoia adapter. The measured stored representation decreased from 46412 to 39163 octets, with unchanged expanded-envelope bytes, hardware keys, ordinary certificates and PIN/touch policies. That lossless test did not exercise ultra-compact reconstruction.

Ultra-compact Java software checks cover fresh-salt reconstruction, key and metadata preservation, cache validation, signing/decryption, 12 malformed authenticated templates rejected before private operations, and 60 injected storage/recovery interruption points. A synthetic two-User-ID companion measured 43918 octets in full compressed storage and 15431 octets in ultra-compact storage. These are software-fixture encoded sizes, not measurements of a physical-device conversion or a guarantee of recoverable card space. Physical ultra-compact conversion has not yet been tested.

Independent Java/Rust software interoperability also passed: the Sequoia adapter reconstructed the Java-produced PQMCP002 template through a simulated card backend, using one P-384 unwrap, five certification-key ML-DSA operations and one signing-key ML-DSA operation for the two-User-ID fixture. A subsequent validated public-cache restore succeeded with the private backend unavailable and no new private calls. Java and Sequoia verified each other's signatures and decrypted each other's ciphertexts using the reconstructed certificate. These tests establish software-format interoperability for this profile; they do not establish physical-device reconstruction timing or touch behavior.

The accompanying public software fixture uses synthetic identities and a synthetic serial; no private keys or actual user's hardware backup are included. It exercises pure and composite envelope signatures, compressed framing, and separated certification/signing keys. The extension payload, other-card bindings, and all possible certificate algorithms require additional implementation and interoperability testing.

section.name: Proposed Future-Creation Layout
section.t: This planning note is not an implemented mapping, a migration instruction, or a replacement for the current companion bindings. A future initial-provisioning layout could group roles as follows: 9c/9d for PQ message signing/decryption; 82/83 for PQ/classical certification; 84/85 for classical S/MIME signing/ECDH; 86/87 for classical Edwards/Montgomery OpenPGP signing/ECDH; 88/89 for standalone classical compatibility; and 8a/8b for the additional ML-KEM-768/X25519 encryption components of a Level 5 v4 compatibility certificate. Algorithms would depend on the selected profile, unused slots would remain empty, and a software component would have no fictitious hardware slot.

Such a layout needs a distinct, versioned, signed manifest before deployment. In particular, assigning certification to slot 82 conflicts with the current companion's P-384 wrapping role in that slot. Existing PQMCP001/PQMCP002 mappings MUST retain their current meaning; a reader MUST NOT reinterpret them according to this proposal. No key move, regeneration, policy change or provisioning operation is authorized by this note. New-layout support and tests require a later explicit specification revision.

section.name: Synthetic Public Test Material
section.t: The repository accompanying this draft includes a public-only software fixture, a framing validator, and build instructions. The fixture contains both pure-signed and composite-signed compressed base bundles and the expected component SPKIs. It MUST NOT be used as a production identity. The framing validator does not replace cryptographic signature verification; independent signature validation uses the Sequoia adapter test suite.

Negative tests should include truncated chunks, wrong indices/generations, digest mismatch, invalid zlib boundaries, expansion overflow, trailing bytes, invalid signatures in either composite component, secret OpenPGP packets, invalid bindings, wrong device or key, conflicting mappings, unknown critical extensions, namespace collisions, and interruption after every mutation step. A public-only reader must not perform a private-key operation or confer contact trust. An ultra-compact reconstruction test must establish explicit authorization and prove that malformed templates are rejected before private-key operations.
